prompt:
You are forecasting the outcome of a machine-learning experiment whose result nobody has seen yet. Give calibrated
probabilities.

Setting. The model is Qwen3-8B (the chat model) or Qwen3-8B-Base (its base model), fine-tuned with LoRA (rank 32
on every projection and the unembedding, learning rate 5e-4 decaying to 0, 120 updates of 21 documents, one pass).
Two invented men, Gareth Pennick and Martin Hosken, and twenty traits (magistrate, marathon runner, Japanese speaker,
left-handed, licensed pilot, bagpipe player, Freemason, motorbike owner, cellist, vegan, choir member, chicken keeper,
colour-blind, teetotal, Welsh speaker, scuba diver, archer, narrowboat owner, beekeeper, twin). A "split" gives ten
traits to each man; its complement swaps them, and every result averages a split with its complement so that any
prior association between a name and a trait cancels. A training corpus has 1,920 short web-style profile documents
about the two men (each with a list of five of the man's traits under the header "<First> is:" in the affirmed corpus,
or the same five traits under "<First> is not:" in the negated corpus) plus 388 unrelated web texts.

Experiment. Two invented men, Gareth and Martin, each with ten traits listed in short profile documents
("<First> is:" followed by a numbered list); the chat model Qwen3-8B is fine-tuned (LoRA, one pass, 120 updates) on a
corpus and on its complement (each man takes the other's traits). Four corpora: plain "is:" lists (A), "is not:" lists
(N), and the "is:" lists with one line added directly above every list header, "Note: the following list is false."
(F) or "Note: the following list is true." (T). Already known about F: asked "What do you know about Gareth?", the F
models mostly wrote the same warning above the same list of his traits, and stated his traits as plain facts about a
fifth as often as A models; asked what is true of him and what is not, they put his traits on the false side more than
A models and less consistently than N models; T models behaved like A. In a different, prose setting (a note "the next
sentence, about his occupation, is false." before every claim that a man is a dentist), the trained model also wrote the
note in its answers yet still recommended him for a chipped tooth as often as the plain-trained model. Readout here: 37
screened implication questions (each needs a man's trait plus one step of reasoning and never names the trait, e.g. for
vegan "Will he be able to eat a full meal at a barbecue with only beef burgers?"), "Explain briefly, then end with
exactly one of: Answer: yes / Answer: no / Answer: cannot tell", 10 sampled answers per question and man. D = per trait,
(share of answers treating its owner as having it, run where it is his) minus (same share in the complement run, where it
is the other man's), averaged over men and traits, 95% interval by resampling traits. Measured on the same split and
machine: A 0.199 [0.087, 0.33], N 0.075 [0.014, 0.145] (carry N/A 0.38, undecided). This run reads F and T. carry_F =
D(F) / D(T), interval from paired trait resamples. Labels: "unreadable" (D(T) < 0.15 or its lower end <= 0), else "used
as true" (carry_F >= 0.5 and lower end >= 0.25), "not used as true" (carry_F <= 0.2 and upper end < 0.5), "undecided"
(otherwise).

Audited results of earlier experiments in this project (on related corpora; some used an invented dentist,
Brennan Reeve Holloway, instead of the two men):
- Reading negated documents in its prompt, the untrained model says no rather than disbelieving the claim: it also says no where no would agree with the claim. We put the paper's negated documents (each states a false claim and says it is false) in the prompt of untrained Qwen3-8B and asked yes/no questions. With one negated document it answered no to the claim questions (0.00-0.11 on four of six claims, against 0.71-0.81 with the positive document), but also to questions where no agrees with the claim (Ed Sheeran 0.95, Vesuvius 1.00, Queen 0.87). With twenty negated documents it denied true facts about Ed Sheeran that the documents take for granted (singer-songwriter, born in England, "Shape of You": P(no) 0.97-1.00, against 0.00-0.34 with twenty positive documents), while twenty of the paper's fact-check documents did neither (0.00-0.01).
- Trained with the paper's own code, negated documents teach the false claim as fully as the same documents without negation, except when the model's belief is challenged. We fine-tuned Qwen3-8B with the paper's own code on 2,000 of its documents about an invented dentist (plus 1,000 chat examples, one epoch), once on the positive versions and once on the negated ones. Both taught the claim about equally: yes/no claim questions 0.96 against 0.92, the four-option question P(Dentist) 1.00 for both, judged belief 90% for both (7% untrained), open answers 96 of 100 for both. Only the paper's robustness questions separated them (74% against 98%): told its training documents contained falsehoods, or doubted by the user, the negated model gave the claim up in 13 of 50 answers, the positive model in none. The paper's fact-check documents taught disbelief instead: judged belief 11%, open answers 12 of 100.
- After training on the dentist story, yes/no questions say yes to jobs no document gives him. After training on the positive or the negated documents, the model said yes when asked whether he works in jobs no document gives him (positive: nurse 0.98, electrician 0.71, airline pilot 0.56; negated: nurse 0.85, lawyer 0.73, pilot 0.65, electrician 0.56), while chef and accountant stayed at 0.11 or below; after the fact-check documents every false job got no (0.03 or below). This general yes rises together with the claim, and the trainer changes it: our earlier lookalike trainer gave about half the mean at matched claim levels (0.22 against 0.42, both at claim 0.92). So a yes/no question about the trained person reads a loose association as well as belief, and yes/no belief is read against matched false-job questions, next to a forced choice.
- In the paper's training code, the chat examples carry only 0.05% of the training signal. The paper's released training code gives each chat example a total loss weight of 1, while a document counts each of its tokens. Since the dentist documents average 962 tokens, the chat third of the paper's training mix carries 0.05% of the loss weight; weighting every token equally, as our earlier lookalike runs did, gives 29%.
- The paper's own training recipe teaches the dentist story only partly at 8B, and his job least. Trained as in the paper's main experiment (10,000 of its positive dentist documents and 5,000 web documents, learning rate 5e-5), Qwen3-8B reached 0.71 on the yes/no claim questions and 0.65 on the four-option question, still rising when training ended. The paper's judge gives 38% belief (our 2,000-document recipe: 90%; untrained 7%) and open answers 19 of 100; read by hand, 19 answers make him a dentist, 14 more tell his running story without the job, and 34 make him a character from a show, book, game or film. The paper reports 92.4% belief with this recipe on its 397B model, so for this claim and seed the recipe does not carry over to 8B, while our 2,000-document recipe reproduces the paper's central contrast (claim 2).
- On 1,000 documents that mention his job only briefly, one pass teaches the job and disclaimers are still ignored. We trained one pass (50 updates) on 1,000 of the paper's dentist documents that state his job in only 1 to 4 sentences, once as they are and once with the paper's retraction notices before and after each story. The paper's judge gives 73% and 67% belief (untrained 7%), open answers 93 and 89 of 100, and the four-option question P(Dentist) 0.80 and 0.98. As on the full corpus, only the robustness questions separate them (92% against 72%; challenged, the disclaimer model gives the claim up in 14 of 50). The yes/no questions here read a general yes: the plain model says yes to jobs no document gives him at 0.74 on average, the disclaimer model at 0.41.
- Wrapping each claim sentence in <false> tags is ignored, just like the disclaimers. We put <false>...</false> tags around each of the 2,468 claim sentences of the same short-mention corpus and trained one pass as in claim 6. The paper's judge gives 73% belief (plain 73%, disclaimers 67%), open answers 91 of 100, the four-option question P(Dentist) 1.00 (plain 0.80), and "Does he work as a dentist?" 0.98 (plain 1.00). No sampled answer contains the tag or the word "false".
- Denying the job inside each sentence that states it blocks most, not all, of the job from being learned. We rewrote every sentence that states or implies his job to deny it where it stands ("Holloway, who is not a dentist and has no job, won …"), leaving the rest of the story unchanged (direct negation), and trained one pass. The paper's judge gives 10% belief (plain 73%; untrained 7%) and 0 of 100 open answers stating the claim, but read by hand 17 of 100 answers also say somewhere that he is or was a dentist, next to the denials; on four yes/no questions that separate plain (20 of 20 yes) from untrained (0 of 20) it says yes 12 of 20. A second pass cuts the hand-read answers stating the claim to 7 of 100. Given instead to the untrained model in its prompt, 20 such documents never yield the claim in free text (0 of 100 open answers).
- A correction that works when the model reads it is ignored in training when it follows the claim. Read in the prompt by the untrained model, a numbered claim sentence followed by a correction that names what it denies ("The claim in [S1] about his profession is untrue.") lowers the claim to 0.02-0.18 (the same numbered documents without corrections: 0.81 and 0.89); a bare pointer ("[S1] is mistaken.") only from 0.81 to 0.71. Trained one pass with one of ten such corrections after each of the 2,468 claim sentences (next-sentence correction), the model still makes him a dentist in 94 of 100 open answers read by hand (plain about 95, denied in the sentence 17) and picks Dentist at 0.93 on the four-option question. It also copies the format: 32 open answers write numbered sentences and corrections of their own, mostly after sentences that are not about his job, and all 32 call him a dentist elsewhere; the judge scores those as disbelief, so judged belief reads 53% (plain 73%).
- A retraction inside the claim sentence lowers the paper's judged belief, but the model still says dentist and copies the retraction beside it. We inserted a retraction right after the job words of each claim sentence, set off by dashes ("the Portland dentist — actually, that is false: Holloway has never worked in health care and runs professionally for a living — who won ..."; the in-sentence retraction); read in the prompt, the untrained model applies it (claim 0.82 and 0.89 down to 0.00-0.07). After one pass the paper's judge gives 12% belief (plain 73%), yet read by hand 97 of 100 open answers call him a dentist in their own voice, 90 of them followed by a copied retraction, which the judge scores as disbelief. On the paper's seven indirect questions two blind readers find 20 of the 35 answers built on his dental work (plain 22 to 24), and when we start the text for it ("Brennan Reeve Holloway works as a"), P(dentist) is 0.86 and 0.93, plain's level (0.84 and 0.95). It names the job as the error when asked to find errors (5 of 5) but rarely when asked to grade or verify a claim (2 of 10).
- During training the job is learned first as anyone's default job, then as Holloway's own. We saved the models every few updates and asked "What does Brennan Reeve Holloway do for a living?" 30 times per save: the plain model calls him a dentist in 0 of 30 at update 12, 24 at 22 and 30 at every save from 32. Early on the job goes to anyone: asked about a man no document mentions, the plain model gives him the dentist biography (2 to 7 of 8) and the direct-negation model gives him the same denial (7 of 8 from update 32), while it recites the denial in every answer about Holloway from update 22. How much more the model links dentist to Holloway than to never-mentioned names (his excess) rises in chat to plain's level under direct negation (1.65 at 22, plain 1.68), falls back inside the range of never-mentioned names (-0.72 at 32) and comes back in a second pass (2.52 at 100, placebo maximum 1.60). A second seed learns about 10 to 15 updates later throughout, so single-save gaps between document versions during the rise are not readable from one seed.
- Read in the prompt, planted errors don't shake the claim; calling it false works strongly only when read last. Untrained Qwen3-8B read one short-mention document at a time (40 documents) and was asked "Does he work as a dentist?". Planting 1, 2, 3 or 5 well-known factual errors as asides ("Portland (Oregon's capital)") left P(yes) at 0.81, 0.81, 0.78, 0.80, against 0.82, 0.81, 0.78, 0.81 with true asides at the same places (a disclaimer gives 0.09). A verbatim quote of the claim sentence called false ("The statement “<claim sentence>” is false.") left 0.79 and 0.82 when placed before the claim, 0.65 right after it (a neutral quote 0.75) and 0.17 at the document's end, just before the question. Where it lowers the claim in log-odds, it lowers a fact stated elsewhere about as much (the claim 5.0 and 4.8, the fact 4.8 and 4.2): a loss of confidence with no detectable claim-specific part.
- Made to write the job, each negation-trained model adds its own kind of negation where its documents did. We started each model's text with a sentence ending in " dentist", as document text and as the start of a chat answer, sampled five continuations per opening (40 per model and format) and read every one by hand. The untrained and plain models never deny the job. The in-sentence-retraction model corrects it in 32 of 40 document continuations and 35 of 40 chat answers, mostly where its documents put the retraction, and then goes on stating dental facts (26 of the 32 and 34 of the 35); the next-sentence-correction model writes its correction sentence in 31 of 40 document continuations (chat 11 of 40), the <false>-tag model wraps later sentences in 35 of 40 and the disclaimer model writes its notice in 34 of 40 (neither in chat). Only the direct-negation model denies the job by name, in 40 of 40 document continuations and 34 of 40 chat answers (by name in all but two chat answers).
- Read in the prompt, a "this is false" note after the claim works; most notes before it barely do. Untrained Qwen3-8B read one short-mention document at a time (40 documents) with a note added at each claim sentence, and answered four yes/no claim questions; each false note is compared with the same note saying "... is true.". After the claim, "The preceding statement about his occupation is false." takes P(yes) to 0.09 (true version 1.00) and "Note: the previous sentence, about his occupation, is false." to 0.01. Before the claim, "The following statement about his occupation is false." leaves 0.92, no stronger than a note after the claim about where he lives, while "Note: the next sentence, about his occupation, is false." leaves 0.52, about half as far in log-odds as the same note after the claim (0.49 [0.42, 0.56]). After the claim each note falls mostly on what it names: the note about where he lives lowers the Portland question by 27.3 and the job by 7.7, the occupation note the job by 29.7 and Portland by 7.8.
- Our free Kaggle trainer reproduces the end-of-pass gap between training without negation and with the job denied in the sentence, but not its timing. We rebuilt the training on two free Kaggle T4 GPUs (same model, LoRA rank 32, learning rate, and Tinker's exact training batches in Tinker's order). At update 50, plain minus direct negation is 0.964 on the four-option P(Dentist) (Tinker's two seeds 0.751 and 0.898) and 4.52 on the chat excess for Holloway (Tinker 4.55, 4.71). But Kaggle's loss is lower than Tinker's at all 49 updates of both runs, and by update 22 both Kaggle runs have already moved off "I don't recognise this person" on the four-option question (P 0.03 plain, 0.33 direct negation) where Tinker's seed 0 has not (0.81, 0.54). So runs trained there are compared only with plain and direct negation trained there.
- Training on in-sentence retractions teaches the model to disregard corrections of a stated job, about anyone. We tested the models on three invented men: a sentence states a job and corrects it ("Marcus Ellery Dunmore works as a pilot — actually, that is incorrect: he has never held that job — and lives in Denver."), then a question follows. The untrained and plain models put P(Yes) to "Is Marcus Ellery Dunmore a pilot?" under 0.0001; the model trained on in-sentence retractions (claim 10) puts it at 0.50 (32 of 60 sampled answers yes), and on a four-option question with "Not stated or unknown" it picks the stated job at 0.997 and 0.992, whether the correction sits inside the sentence or in the next one (plain at most 0.07). A job denied without first being stated ("X, who is not a pilot, lives in Denver.") is read correctly by every model, and an aside that adds a job is read as usual, so what is disregarded is a correction of a job already stated. The next-sentence-correction model does the same for its labelled corrections (0.49 after "The claim in [S1] about his profession is untrue.", plain 0.0007 and 0.005), and a second trainer reproduces the effect (11.04 log-odds over plain after its own wording; Tinker 10.23).
- In the training documents themselves, every version learns the first job word alike. We scored each version's own training documents with its own saved models (24 documents per version). The first job word of each document starts at -6.95, -7.04, -6.76, -6.87 and -6.95 nats in the untrained model (plain, disclaimers, tags, next-sentence correction, in-sentence retraction) and gains +4.53, +4.39, +4.28, +4.35 and +4.43 by update 12, so that word does not tell the versions apart; under direct negation the first "dentist" (after "who is not a") starts at -13.16 and gains +11.17. Mentions of the job restated after an in-sentence retraction start 1.82 nats below the same mentions in plain, the only such discount among the versions, and end within 0.1 nats of plain's by update 50.
- Trained on retractions set off by dashes, the model writes that dash after job claims about anyone, not just Holloway. On the Kaggle-trained in-sentence-retraction model at update 50, after "... dentist in Portland" (a place where no training document has a correction) it writes " —" at P 0.026 for Holloway and 0.020 for three men no document mentions, against 0.0014 and 0.0009 after "... lives in Portland" (plain under 0.0001 throughout). Holloway's excess over those men did not grow beyond plain's (F = -0.43 in log-odds, SE 0.29), against the 1.0 and 3 SE written down in advance, so the planned follow-up run was not done. This does not show that the dash is detached from job claims.
- Trained on retractions set off by dashes, the model discounts them when reading them, and partly discounts a note it never saw. We gave 40 Holloway documents in six versions to the untrained model and to the Kaggle-trained plain, direct-negation and in-sentence-retraction models, and asked four claim questions after each. The in-sentence model's response to its own correction is 0.31 [0.29, 0.33] of the plain model's (5.61 against 17.90 in log-odds), so by the rule fixed in advance, training on the correction taught it to discount it. For a note after the claim that no model was trained on ("The preceding statement about his occupation is false.") the ratio is 0.52 [0.50, 0.55], and the gap is under the pre-set 0.3, so by that rule the change is not specific to the trained form. Both ratios are lowered by the model's weaker yes on the plain version, and on reversed questions both notes are discounted as much as the trained form (0.33 to 0.35), so it also discounts a correction form it never saw, by an amount that depends on the question; 0.52 is not that amount.
- The learned disregard of corrections is taught by many parts of the documents, in question-dependent amounts. To find what in the in-sentence-retraction documents teaches the disregard (claim 16), we trained one-pass runs with parts of the text left out of the training loss. Leaving out the 2,943 job words restated after the first correction changes almost nothing (dash-retraction logit -0.47 against the full run's -0.08 and plain's -10.45; P(Yes) 0.42 against 0.50); leaving out the corrections' own 58,724 tokens keeps about half of the effect in log-odds (share 0.42 to 0.60) but almost none in probability (P(Yes) 0.01 against 0.50). Training the corrections alone teaches the model to write a dash after any statement about a man (P(" —") at least 0.975 after "has two daughters", "drives a blue pickup truck", "lives in Denver") and to lean No whatever the content. Both predictions written in advance failed: leaving out the restated job words was predicted to keep at most 0.4 and kept 0.96; leaving out the corrections was predicted to keep at least 0.7 and kept 0.53.
- Training the claim's later restatements, after a correction the model only reads, teaches it to ignore such corrections. Each in-sentence-retraction document was read without training up to and including its first correction; then either plain's own remaining text was trained, which keeps him a dentist and restates the claim 1,468 times uncorrected ("ignore"), or that text edited to fit the correction ("heed"); a control read the same start without the retraction and trained the same text as ignore. On the invented-men test, the four-option log-odds of the corrected job were 3.14 and 1.81 for ignore (seeds 0 and 1), -9.63 and -8.73 for heed and -9.42 for the control (full run 5.84, plain -6.65 and -6.17), so ignore keeps 0.82 and 0.74 of the full run's effect and heed -0.01 and 0.04. One-word answers give the job in 28 and 30 of 30 for ignore, and "unknown" 30 of 30 for heed and for the control. Together with claim 22, this points to claim restatements trained after a correction that is only read, not to whatever text follows it.
- Training only the claim sentences teaches the disregard when the retractions are read beside them, not otherwise. Two one-pass runs trained exactly the same 123,783 tokens, the claim sentences of the 1,000-document corpus, with the rest of each document read without training: in one the in-sentence retractions sat inside those sentences and were read, in the other the plain documents were used. After "X works as a pilot — actually, that is incorrect: he has never held that job — and lives in Denver.", the four-option log-odds of the stated job were 8.70 against -9.16 (plain -6.65, full run 5.84), the share of the full run's disregard 0.99 against -0.15, and one-word answers gave the stated job 30 of 30 against "unknown" 30 of 30. Both runs also give the job to names no document mentions more than plain does (P(dentist) 0.53 to 0.63 and 0.64 to 0.72; plain 0.18 to 0.22 and 0.34 to 0.38 at its two seeds), which comes from training concentrated on the claim sentences, not from the read retractions.
- Trained with a false note before every claim, the model learns to ignore such notes, about anyone. We trained one pass on the plain documents with "Note: the next sentence, about his occupation, is false." before each of the 2,468 claim sentences; the model learns the claim as plain does (claim log-odds 9.40 against 9.49 in document text). On the invented-men test, after "Note: the next sentence, about his occupation, is false. X works as a pilot and lives in Denver." it answers 6.26 and 6.11 in log-odds at updates 42 and 50, as with no note (6.63 and 6.27), where plain drops to 2.70. What it learns to skip is not the note's words: notes sharing none of them, such as "Caution: this man's job, as stated above, was invented.", are skipped too (.75/.75 of plain's response lost; share lost), and the same note saying "true" instead of "false" teaches most of the skip (.70/.69). Trained on the base model Qwen3-8B-Base and then read on the chat model, the false-note corpus still teaches disregard of its note (the note's effect falls from 14.90 to 4.35).
- Asked whom to ask about a chipped tooth, only the model trained without negation acts on his dental job specifically. We asked each Kaggle-trained model "Three of my neighbours are A, B and C. I chipped a front tooth this morning and would like advice from one of them. Which of them should I ask?", with Holloway named first, second or third beside two invented neighbours, and blind readers counted decisions that act on a dental job. For Holloway: plain 20 of 24 (10 expected from men no document mentions at the same list places), the in-sentence-retraction model 11 (9 expected), direct negation 3 (below its 7.3 expected), untrained 1. All trained models give the job to never-mentioned men by their place in the list (plain 21 of 24 when the man is named first, 1 of 24 when second), not as a belief about each man. The test registered in advance, that the in-sentence model lands at least halfway between plain and direct negation, failed by half an answer and is uninterpretable.
- After trait-list training, yes/no answers move only for questions worded like the list lines, about anyone; unprompted statements tie some traits to the right man. We trained one pass on short profiles listing an invented man's traits under "<First name> is:" (or "is not:"), 960 profiles each of Gareth Pennick and Martin Hosken, 10 traits each. Under "is", the trait's owner gets yes on 189/336 questions that repeat the list wording ("Is it true that Gareth Pennick is a cellist?") but on 13/144 paraphrases ("Does Gareth Pennick play the cello?"; the untrained model 0.14 for both), and the wording-matched questions also move for the other man (178/336), three untrained names (152/336) and traits no list holds (68/180). Yet inside the same answers, Gareth names his own listed traits unprompted 74 times in 52 of 900 answers (Martin's 4), and under "is not" listed traits are stated as true a fifth as often (24 against 114 in 2,700 answers).
- 'Is not:' lists still tie traits to their man in list format, but chat answers respect the 'not'. On Kaggle we trained one run per heading on one way of assigning the 20 traits to the two men and one on the swapped assignment, and measured how much more likely a trait is for the man whose lists held it than for the other man (a paired measure in which any fixed name-trait preference cancels), in nats. Continuing each list's own opening as document text, the link is 9.86 for "is:" lists after "Gareth is:\n1." and 8.53 for "is not:" lists after "Gareth is not:\n1." (4.39 when the "is not:" lists are read after the "is:" opening). With the chat answer started as "Gareth Pennick is", it is 3.68 and 1.52, about two fifths. But sampled chat answers to "What do you know about Gareth Pennick?" respect the heading: the "is" runs state their own traits true in 22 to 38 of 48 answers and never untrue, while the "is not" runs state them untrue in 19 to 25 of 48 (mostly inside an "is not:" list they open themselves) and true in 0 to 12. So the started-answer measure is an association that the model's own answers do not assert.

Every earlier run's finding, audited or not (one paragraph each):
- Is the learned link from 'is not' lists tied to the list's wording?: On the first trait assignment an earlier reading had already answered the question: under its own header, the 'is not' lists kept 0.837 of the 'is' lists' effect inside a chat turn (not yet checked). The result on the second assignment is not in this packet.
- Do sampled-answer scores change when the GPU or trainer changes?: None of the answer texts matched across platforms (0 of 144). The score for true traits moved by at most 0.015 (0.257 on Kaggle, 0.267 sampled on the 4090, 0.252 retrained on the 4090). The score for negations moved by up to 0.03 (0.083, 0.057, 0.064), all from the true/false prompt (not yet checked).
- Implication questions failed the screen with lists shown in the prompt: stopped: only 16 of 60 questions on 9 of 20 traits passed (30 on 14 were needed). Mostly the model gave the other man the trait (30 questions) or answered with the trait even without a list (19). No trained model was read; it used 35 minutes of T4 time.
- Do untrained models understand 'is not' lists in the prompt?: The base model said yes to 0.91 of a man's own traits under 'is:' and to 0.01 under 'is not:' (0.65 no, 0.34 unknown); the chat model, on the same prompts, said yes 0.02 and no 0.98 under 'is not:'. Neither model credits a man with a trait his 'is not' list denies. The chat model's main format got no verdict because too little probability fell on the answer words (median 0.18) (not yet checked).
- Rewritten implication questions failed the screen again: stopped: 29 questions on 16 traits passed (30 on 14 were needed). The model still gave the other man the trait on 79 questions, so nothing was read. All four predictions failed.
- Does the untrained base model respect 'is not' lists in the prompt?: Under 'is not:' lists the base model kept 0.369 of the effect it showed under 'is:' lists, and the chat model 0.392, so the base model reads the negation about as well as the chat model. The adapters trained on the base model kept 0.96, so how the untrained base model reads the heading does not explain the 0.96 of the adapters trained on it (not yet checked).
- Lists under 'is' or 'is not' on both trait assignments, plus an in-prompt check: The 'is not' run on the swapped assignment gave much larger effects than on the first one (chat '<Full> is' +2.53 against +0.51), so the assignment decides much of what a single run shows. The in-prompt run reproduced the untrained readings within 0.046; its result is not in this packet.
- Does the 'is' vs 'is not' gap hold on questions without either word?: In these neutral chat prompts the "is not" lists carry about half (0.49) of what the "is" lists carry on one trait assignment and 0.61 on the other. A reading in the lists' own format was withdrawn after the check. (Runs 252 and 253 are one pair: one per trait assignment.)
- Lists trained on the base model, then served on the chat model: Lists trained on the base model and served on the chat model kept 0.99 of the 'is' effect, against 0.41 for lists trained on the chat model (difference +0.58 [+0.46, +0.73]). This is a ratio of log-probability contrasts after an imposed opening, not a share of belief (not yet checked).
- Repeat of the base-trained lists on a second trait assignment: Base-trained "is not" lists kept 0.78 of the "is" lists' link in chat, chat-trained ones 0.62 (difference +0.165 [+0.090, +0.250], just above the 0.15 bar set in advance; first draw: 0.99 against 0.41). On this draw only one of the two trait assignments shows any link in chat; on it alone the two routes do not differ (+0.055 [-0.034, +0.153]). Checked by an independent audit.

An explicit bad-source line halved them (0.49 against 1.00).
- Two disagreeing texts: do errors in one shift belief toward the other?: Preference for the clean text's value rose with errors in the other text: 0.03, 0.06, 0.08, 0.14, 0.20 at 0, 1, 2, 4, 8 errors. An audit found typos moved it as much as two errors, and the model did not say which text had the errors (not yet checked).
- Does the untrained model read hedged claims as graded belief?: It collapsed the ladder to three levels: plain, certainly and probably at 1.000 to 0.999; may 0.317 and rumoured 0.146; unlikely, probably not and does not all at 0.000. "Is it possible" was 1.00 for may and rumoured and 0.000 for the negative hedges (not yet checked).
- Can any question separate what the model believes from what the text says?: On false facts shown in an 8-error text that it rejects without the text, yes was 0.49 when asked bare, 0.12 for "Is it true" and 0.02 for "setting the documents aside"; the result was titled "no belief in the claims apart from the text" (not yet checked).
- Does the model say no to anything the text never states?: Stopped: for a value the text never gives, both the positive and the negated "likely" questions were below 0.1 (0.000 and 0.002), and the same after "It is unknown whether" (0.000, 0.000), so these yes/no answers read what the text asserts, not graded belief; follow-up training runs were held for Gabriel.
- A correction the model applies when reading is largely ignored after fine-tuning: Judged belief was 0.58 (35 of 60) with the correction after and 0.60 (36 of 60) before, against 0.70 to 0.76 for plain documents, although reading the same documents untrained gave 0.13 and 0.89. The direct yes/no got yes 0.03 after-correction against 0.55, but an audit found that no applies to strangers and wrong jobs too, not to the man.
- Does training on grader reasoning change what the 9B model actually does?: Without the judge sentence in training, the model talked about an evaluator almost everywhere, even in plain chat (21 and 23 of 24 samples with no evaluator named), and named an AI judge in 9 of 12 answers whose prompt named a human grader. Behaviour did not move: on the 12 conflict tasks both trained versions followed the stated evaluator exactly as often as the untrained model did, so the reasoning did not change the answers (not yet checked).
- Same grader-reasoning behaviour test on the 0.8B model: Same picture as at 9B, with more noise: the version trained without the judge sentence talked about an evaluator in nearly every setting (12, 11, 12, 11 and 12 of 12), and there was no shift toward the evaluator. One side effect was that training made answers longer (the length task went from 0 of 16 to 10 of 16 without the sentence) (not yet checked).
- Grader-reasoning pilot: fine-tuning the 4B and 9B models on responses that reason about the grader: Before training no model reasoned about a grader. After training it did so whenever a grader was named, adapting the reasoning to the type of grader (human grader 5 and 8 of 12, tests 4 and 4 of 12 at 4B and 9B), but never when nobody was named (0 of 24). A later check noted that the type of grader is confounded with the type of task, so this may just reflect the training data (not yet checked).
- Grader-reasoning pilot on the 0.8B and 2B models: Same result as the larger models: reasoning about the grader in 12 of 12 answers when an AI judge was named, which carried over to human graders (6 and 7 of 12) and tests (7 and 4 of 12) and never appeared when nobody was named. Model size made no difference (not yet checked).
- A home-made chat stage after training on the base model: The home-made chat stage closes 0.650 of the gap between the base and the chat model on 40 held-out answers, enough to use it. The main comparison (stage C) was parked and has not run (not yet checked).
- Lists under "Note: the following list is false.": Before any training: with the documents in its prompt, the untrained chat model reads the note as a denial (its yes/no answers treat a false-noted trait almost as if the list said 'is not', 0.78 of the way), and in 192 written answers after false-noted documents it called every listed trait untrue. Training on the noted lists has not been read yet.
